verses.zh: 论泰尔的默示：他施的船只都要哀号；因为泰尔变为荒场，甚至没有房屋，没有可进之路。这消息是从基提地得来的。
verses.en: This is an oracle[NOTE:1] about Tyre:Wail, you large ships,[NOTE:2] for the port is too devastated to enter![NOTE:3] From the land of Cyprus[NOTE:4] this news is announced to them.
notes: See note at Isa 13:1.
Heb “ships of Tarshish.” This probably refers to large ships either made in or capable of traveling to the distant, western port of Tarshish.

The Hebrew text reads literally, “for it is destroyed, from a house, from entering.” The translation assumes that the mem (מ) on בַּיִת (bayit) was originally an enclitic mem suffixed to the preceding verb. This assumption allows one to take בַּיִת as the subject of the preceding verb. It is used in a metaphorical sense for the port city of Tyre. The preposition min (מִן) prefixed to בּוֹא (boʾ) indicates negative consequence: “so that no one can enter.” See BDB 583 s.v. מִן 7.b.
Heb “the Kittim,” a designation for the people of Cyprus. See HALOT 504-05 s.v. כִּתִּיִּים.

verses.zh: 沿海的居民，就是素来靠航海西顿的商家得丰盛的，你们当静默无言。
verses.en: Lament,[NOTE:1] you residents of the coast,you merchants of Sidon[NOTE:2] who travel over the sea,whose agents sail over
notes: Or “keep quiet”; NAB “Silence!”
For location see Map1-A1; JP3-F3; JP4-F3.

verses.zh: 在大水之上，西曷的粮食、尼罗河的庄稼是泰尔的进项；她作列国的大码头。
verses.en: the deep waters.[NOTE:1] Grain from the Shihor region,[NOTE:2] crops grown near the Nile[NOTE:3] she receives;[NOTE:4] she is the trade center[NOTE:5] of the nations.
notes: The Hebrew text (23:2b-3a) reads literally, “merchant of Sidon, the one who crosses the sea, they filled you, and on the deep waters.” Instead of מִלְאוּךְ (milʾukh, “they filled you”) the Qumran scroll 1QIsaa reads מלאכיך (“your messengers”). The translation assumes an emendation of מִלְאוּךְ to מַלְאָכָו (malʾakhav, “his messengers”), taking the vav (ו) on וּבְמַיִם (uvemayim) as improperly placed; instead it should be the final letter of the preceding word.
Heb “seed of Shihor.” “Shihor” probably refers to the east branch of the Nile. See Jer 2:18 and BDB 1009 s.v. שִׁיחוֹר.
Heb “the harvest of the Nile.”
Heb “[is] her revenue.”
Heb “merchandise”; KJV, ASV “a mart of nations”; NLT “the merchandise mart of the world.”

verses.zh: 西顿哪，你当惭愧；因为大海说，就是海中的保障说：我没有劬劳，也没有生产，没有养育男子，也没有抚养童女。
verses.en: Be ashamed, O Sidon, for the sea[NOTE:1] says this, O fortress of the sea:“I have not gone into labor or given birth;I have not raised young menor brought up young women.”[NOTE:2]
notes: J. N. Oswalt (Isaiah [NICOT], 1:430-31) sees here a reference to Yam, the Canaanite god of the sea. He interprets the phrase מָעוֹז הַיָּם (maʿoz hayyam, “fortress of the sea”) as a title of Yam, translating “Mighty One of the Sea.” A more traditional view is that the phrase refers to Sidon.

Or “virgins” (KJV, ASV, NAB, NASB).sn The sea is personified here as a lamenting childless woman. The foreboding language anticipates the following announcement of Tyre’s demise, viewed here as a child of the sea, as it were.

verses.zh: 这风声传到埃及；埃及人为泰尔的风声极其疼痛。
verses.en: When the news reaches Egypt,they will be shaken by what has happened to Tyre.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “they will be in pain at the report of Tyre.”

verses.zh: 泰尔人哪，你们当过到他施去；沿海的居民哪，你们都当哀号。
verses.en: Travel to Tarshish!Wail, you residents of the coast!

verses.zh: 这是你们欢乐的城，从上古而有的吗？其中的居民往远方寄居。
verses.en: Is this really your boisterous city[NOTE:1] whose origins are in the distant past[NOTE:2] and whose feet led her to a distant land to reside?
notes: Heb “Is this to you, boisterous one?” The pronoun “you” is masculine plural, like the imperatives in v. 6, so it is likely addressed to the Egyptians and residents of the coast. “Boisterous one” is a feminine singular form, probably referring to the personified city of Tyre.
Heb “in the days of antiquity [is] her beginning.”

verses.zh: 泰尔本是赐冠冕的。她的商家是王子；她的买卖人是世上的尊贵人。遭遇如此是谁定的呢？
verses.en: Who planned this for royal Tyre,[NOTE:1] whose merchants are princes,whose traders are the dignitaries[NOTE:2] of the earth?
notes: The precise meaning of הַמַּעֲטִירָה (hammaʿatirah) is uncertain. The form is a Hiphil participle from עָטַר (ʿatar), a denominative verb derived from עֲטָרָה (ʿatarah, “crown, wreath”). The participle may mean “one who wears a crown” or “one who distributes crowns.” In either case, Tyre’s prominence in the international political arena is in view.
Heb “the honored” (so NASB, NRSV); NIV “renowned.”

verses.zh: 是万军之耶和华所定的！为要污辱一切高傲的荣耀，使地上一切的尊贵人被藐视。
verses.en: The Lord of Heaven’s Armies planned it—to dishonor the pride that comes from all her beauty,[NOTE:1] to humiliate all the dignitaries of the earth.
notes: Heb “the pride of all the beauty.”

verses.zh: 他施的民（原文是女）哪，可以流行你的地，好像尼罗河；不再有腰带拘紧你。
verses.en: Daughter Tarshish, travel back to your land, as one crosses the Nile;there is no longer any marketplace in Tyre.[NOTE:1]
notes: This meaning of this verse is unclear. The Hebrew text reads literally, “Cross over your land, like the Nile, daughter of Tarshish, there is no more waistband.” The translation assumes an emendation of מֵזַח (mezakh, “waistband”) to מָחֹז (makhoz, “harbor, marketplace”; see Ps 107:30). The term עָבַר (ʿavar, “cross over”) is probably used here of traveling over the water (as in v. 6). The command is addressed to personified Tarshish, who here represents her merchants. The Qumran scroll 1QIsaa has עבדי (“work, cultivate”) instead of עִבְרִי (ʿivri, “cross over”). In this case one might translate “Cultivate your land, like they do the Nile region” (cf. NIV, CEV). The point would be that the people of Tarshish should turn to agriculture because they will no longer be able to get what they need through the marketplace in Tyre.

verses.zh: 耶和华已经向海伸手，震动列国。至于迦南，他已经吩咐拆毁其中的保障。
verses.en: The Lord stretched out his hand over the sea,[NOTE:1] he shook kingdoms;he[NOTE:2] gave the order to destroy Canaan’s fortresses.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “his hand he stretched out over the sea.”
Heb “the Lord.” For stylistic reasons the pronoun (“he”) has been used in the translation here.
Heb “concerning Canaan, to destroy her fortresses.” NIV, NLT translate “Canaan” as “Phoenicia” here.

verses.zh: 他又说：受欺压西顿的居民（原文是处女）哪，你必不得再欢乐。起来！过到基提去；就是在那里也不得安歇。
verses.en: He said,“You will no longer celebrate,oppressed[NOTE:1] virgin daughter Sidon!Get up, travel to Cyprus,but you will find no relief there.”[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “violated, raped,” the point being that Daughter Sidon has lost her virginity in the most brutal manner possible.
Heb “[to the] Kittim, get up, cross over; even there there will be no rest for you.” On “Kittim” see the note on “Cyprus” at v. 1.

verses.zh: （看哪，迦勒底人之地向来没有这民，这国是亚述人为住旷野的人所立的。现在他们建筑戍楼，拆毁泰尔的宫殿，使她成为荒凉。）
verses.en: Look at the land of the Chaldeans,these people who have lost their identity![NOTE:1] The Assyrians have made it a home for wild animals.They erected their siege towers,[NOTE:2] demolished[NOTE:3] its fortresses,and turned it into a heap of ruins.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “this people [that] is not.”
For the meaning of this word, see HALOT 118 s.v. *בַּחוּן.
Or “laid bare.” For the meaning of this word, see HALOT 889 s.v. ערר.
This verse probably refers to the Assyrian destruction of Babylon.

verses.zh: 他施的船只都要哀号，因为你们的保障变为荒场。
verses.en: Wail, you large ships,[NOTE:1] for your fortress is destroyed!
notes: Heb “ships of Tarshish.” See the note at v. 1.

verses.zh: 到那时，泰尔必被忘记七十年，照着一王的年日。七十年后，泰尔的景况必像妓女所唱的歌：
verses.en: At that time[NOTE:1] Tyre will be forgotten for 70 years,[NOTE:2] the typical life span of a king.[NOTE:3] At the end of 70 years Tyre will try to attract attention again, like the prostitute in the popular song:[NOTE:4]
notes: Or “in that day” (KJV). The verb that introduces this verse serves as a discourse particle and is untranslated; see note on “in the future” in 2:2.
The number 70 is probably used in a stereotypical, nonliteral sense here to indicate a long period of time that satisfies completely the demands of God’s judgment.
Heb “like the days of a king.”
Heb “At the end of 70 years it will be for Tyre like the song of the prostitute.”

verses.zh: 你这被忘记的妓女啊，拿琴周流城内，巧弹多唱，使人再想念你。
verses.en: “Take the harp,go through the city,forgotten prostitute!Play it well,play lots of songs,so you’ll be noticed.”[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “so you will be remembered.”

verses.zh: 七十年后，耶和华必眷顾泰尔，她就仍得利息（原文是雇价；下同），与地上的万国交易（原文是行淫）。
verses.en: At the end of 70 years[NOTE:1] the Lord will revive[NOTE:2] Tyre. She will start making money again by selling her services to all the earth’s kingdoms.[NOTE:3]
notes: The verb that introduces this verse serves as a discourse particle and is untranslated; see note on “in the future” in 2:2.
Heb “visit [with favor]” (cf. KJV, NAB, NASB, NRSV); NIV “will deal with.”
Heb “and she will return to her [prostitute’s] wages and engage in prostitution with all the kingdoms of the earth on the face of the earth.”

verses.zh: 她的货财和利息要归耶和华为圣，必不积攒存留；因为她的货财必为住在耶和华面前的人所得，使他们吃饱，穿耐久的衣服。
verses.en: Her profits and earnings will be set apart for the Lord. They will not be stored up or accumulated, for her profits will be given to those who live in the Lord’s presence and will be used to purchase large quantities of food and beautiful clothes.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “for eating to fullness and for beautiful covering[s].”sn The point of this verse, which in its blatant nationalism comes precariously close to comparing the Lord to one who controls or manages a prostitute, is that Tyre will become a subject of Israel and her God. Tyre’s commercial profits will be used to enrich the Lord’s people.

READING CYCLE THREE (see
"Bible
Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- This condemnation of Phoenicia is paralleled in Ezekiel 26-28 and Amos 1:9-10. Tyre
(capital of Phoenicia) was a powerful and wealthy maritime nation, which caused
them to be prideful and self-reliant.

- Because it was such a widespread empire several nations and geographical areas
mourned for the loss of trade.

- ship of Tarshish (i.e. western Mediterranean area), Isa. 23:1,6,14

- coastlands, Isa. 23:2,6

- merchants of Sidon (i.e. second largest Phoenician city), Isa. 23:2

- Egypt, Isa. 23:3,5

- Canaan, Isa. 23:11

- Cyprus, Isa. 23:12

- Notice the number of IMPERATIVES directed at Tyre/Phoenicia.

- wail, Isa. 23:1, BDB 410, KB 413, Hiphil IMPERATIVE,
cf. Isa. 13:6; 14:31; 15:2,3; 16:7 (twice); 65:14

- be silent (lit. "be still"), Isa. 23:2, BDB 198, KB 226, Qal IMPERATIVE

- be ashamed, Isa. 23:4, BDB 101, KB 116, Qal IMPERATIVE,
cf. Isa. 1:29; 19:9; 20:5; 24:23; 26:11; 29:22; 30:5; 37:27; 41:11; 42:17; 44:9,11; 45:16,17,24;
49:23; 50:7; 54:4; 65:13; 66:5; Micah 3:7; 7:16

- pass over, Isa. 23:6, BDB 716, KB 778, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Isa. 23:2

- wail, Isa. 23:6, same as #1

- overflow (lit. "pass over"), Isa. 23:10, same as #4

- arise, Isa. 23:12, BDB 877, KB 1086, Qal IMPERATIVE

- pass over, Isa. 23:12, same as #4,6

- wail, Isa. 23:14, same as #1,5

- take your harp, Isa. 23:16, BDB 542, KB 534, Qal IMPERATIVE

- walk about the city, Isa. 23:16, BDB 685, KB 738, Qal IMPERATIVE

- pluck the strings (lit. "play skillfully"), Isa. 23:16, BDB 405, KB 408, Hiphil
IMPERATIVE, cf. 1 Sam. 16:17; Ps. 33:3; Ezek. 33:32

- sing many songs, v 16, BDB 915, KB 1176, Hiphil IMPERATIVE

- As always in trying to interpret the poems of Isaiah the historical setting would be very
helpful in understanding the details and allusions, but these poems could fit several different
invasions. The book of Isaiah is a collection of messages from throughout his life combined at
some future date (an anthology by Isaiah's disciples). They are structured in non-chronological ways based on

- related words

- related geographical areas

- word plays

- themes

- and more

Moderns do not know how, when, or by whom the OT books were finally compiled/edited.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: ISAIAH 23:1-7

1The oracle concerning Tyre.

Wail, O ships of Tarshish,

For Tyre is destroyed, without house or harbor;

It is reported to them from the land of Cyprus.

2Be silent, you inhabitants of the coastland,

You merchants of Sidon;

Your messengers crossed the sea

3And were on many waters.

The grain of the Nile, the harvest of the River was her revenue;

And she was the market of nations.

4Be ashamed, O Sidon;

For the sea speaks, the stronghold of the sea, saying,

"I have neither travailed nor given birth,

I have neither brought up young men nor reared virgins."

5When the report reaches Egypt,

They will be in anguish at the report of Tyre.

6Pass over to Tarshish;

Wail, O inhabitants of the coastland.

7Is this your jubilant city,

Whose origin is from antiquity,

Whose feet used to carry her to colonize distant places?

23:1 "oracle" See full lexical note at Isa. 13:1.

▣ "Tyre" See Contextual Insights, A. and B.

▣ "Wail, O ships of Tarshish" "Wail" (ילל,
BDB 410, KB 413, Hiphil IMPERATIVE) denotes loud shrieking. It is used often in
Isaiah (cf. Isa. 13:6; 14:31; 15:2,3; 16:7 [twice]; 23:1,6,14; 52:5; 65:14 and a related
term [יללה] in Isa. 15:8 [twice]). See
SPECIAL TOPIC: GRIEVING RITES.

Note this same phrase appears in Isa. 23:14. Often a repeated phrase marks a literary unit, but
here that does not fit well.

The ships of Tarshish were large commercial grain carriers, usually from Egypt. They became an
idiom (as did "Phoenicia" and "Canaanite") for merchants. Here they are personified for literary effect.

▣ "Tarshish" This place name (BDB 1077) could refer to

- a city in southern Spain on the Atlantic side, which was a Phoenician colony (i.e.
Tartessus, possibly modern Sevilla)

- the island of Sardinia (cf. Gen. 10:4)

- a city on the north African coast (Carthage was a colony of Phoenicia)

- a metaphor for a far distant port

- a type of large sea-going commercial ship

- a rival maritime nation (cf. 1 Kgs. 10:22)

SPECIAL TOPIC: TARSHISH (place)

▣ "without house or harbor" The city of Tyre had two inhabited areas.

- most of the houses and shops were located on the mainland coast (cf. Josh. 19:29; 2 Sam. 24:7)

- the palace, temple, and fortress were on an island (originally two small islands) just off the
coast (cf. Ezek. 27:32)

This made it almost invulnerable until Alexander the Great in 332 B.C.
destroyed the coastal part and used the debris to build a causeway to the island fortress (cf. Ezek. 26:3-5).

The ships from Tarshish had no where to offload their cargo, nor receive different cargo to transport.

There is a textual issue with both "house" and "harbor."

- The word "house" in the MT (BDB 108) could also be "harbor" with only a revocalization.

- "without house" (REV) ‒ מבית

- "harbor" (NEB) ‒ מבית

- The word "harbor" is literally a Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT (BDB 97, KB 112)
meaning "to come in," which in this context, denotes coming into a place of anchorage or dock.

Both #1 and #2 seem to refer to the Port of Tyre.

▣ "Cyprus" The MT has "Kittim" (BDB 508), possibly taken from the name of a Roman city on the
island of Cyprus called "Citium," which was originally a Phoenician colony (cf. Isa. 23:7).

Some identify the inhabitants with one of the sons of Javan, Elishah (cf. Gen. 10:4; Ezek. 27:7).

23:2 "Be silent" This Qal IMPERATIVE is parallel to "wail" in
Isa. 23:1 (BDB 198 I). There is speculation based on a Ugaritic root that it reflects a separate root
(BDB 199 II) "lament" ("wail," TEV; "lament," REB).

▣ "Sidon" This was a coastal city (cf. Gen. 10:19) of Phoenicia about twenty-five miles north of
Tyre. It was originally the main city (cf. Josh. 13:4,6). The name seems to have come from the eldest son
of Canaan, son of Ham (cf. Gen. 10:15). Tyre and Sidon are often linked together in the NT in reference
to the nation of Phoenicia (cf. Matt. 11:21,22; 15:21; Acts 12:20).

The MT has "grain of Shihor, harvest of the Nile." Shihor (BDB 1009) means "the pond of
Horus" (KB 1477). It referred to

- an eastern branch of the Nile (BDB 1009)

- a canal of black (BDB 1007 I) water

- a lake in the eastern delta region

It is spelled differently in

- Josh. 13:13; 1 Chr. 13:5, שׁיחור

- Jer. 2:18, שׁחור

- Isa. 23:3, שׁחר

but all refer to the same area in Egypt.

▣ "she was the market of nations" See Ezek. 27:3-23.

23:4 "Be ashamed" The VERB (BDB 101, KB 116, Qal
IMPERATIVE) is used of God's judgment on idols (cf. Jer. 50:2). Here it
denotes the shame of a defeated nation (cf. Isa. 1:29; 19:9; 37:27; 41:11). These nations can experience
forgiveness and restoration if they will turn to YHWH (cf. Isa. 49:23); this is also true of His own people
(cf. Isa. 29:23; 45:17; 54:4).

▣ "Sidon" Sidon is personified. The NRSV footnote says "Ruined Sidon is barren like the sea
without sailors (i.e. young men)."

It is possible that the speaker is not personified Sidon but the Canaannite god, Yam
("sea"). If so, then the next phrase is a characterization of the Canaanite sea god, "Mighty One of the Sea"
(J. Oswalt, Isaiah, pp. 430-431).

23:6 "Tarshish" See
SPECIAL TOPIC: TARSHISH

23:7 This describes Tyre (cf. Isa. 23:5)

- jubilant city (i.e. prideful and self-satisfied, cf. Isa. 22:2; 24:8; 32:13)

- very old city (i.e. pride in their antiquity)

- colonizing nation (pride in their international influence)

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: ISAIAH 23:8-11

8Who has planned this against Tyre, the bestower of crowns,

Whose merchants were princes, whose traders were the honored of the earth?

9The Lord of hosts has planned it, to defile the pride of all beauty,

To despise all the honored of the earth.

10Overflow your land like the Nile, O daughter of Tarshish,

There is no more restraint.

11He has stretched His hand out over the sea,

He has made the kingdoms tremble;

The Lord has given a command concerning Canaan to demolish its strongholds.

23:8-12 This strophe is united by the use of the VERB "planned" (lit.
"advised" or "purposed," BDB 419, KB 421, Qal PERFECT, cf. Isa. 23:8,9;
14:24, 26, 27; 19:12,17). There is an intentionality behind history-YHWH! The kingdoms of this world
make their plans (Isa. 23:8), but the God of creation also makes His (Isa. 23:9).

23:12 In this chapter Phoenicia (NIV) is called by the name of its old capital, "Sidon," and also
its new current capital, "Tyre."

▣ "Arise, pass over to Cyprus; even there you will find no rest" Some see this as referring
specifically to the king of Sidon, "Lulli," fleeing from the Assyrian army to Cyprus in
701 B.C., where he was killed (JB footnote, p. 1177). This is surely
possible, but not certain. Hebrew poetry is ambiguous.

23:13 "the land of the Chaldeans" This seems to refer to the destruction of old Babylon (not Neo-Babylon)
by Assyria (cf. chapters 13-14). There are two "Babylons" mentioned in the Prophets.

- small semi-autonomous region close to the mouth of the Tigris and Euphrates rivers that
rebelled against Assyria and was invaded and their capital "Babylon" destroyed by
Sargon II (722-705 B.C.), who took the Babylonian throne
name "King of Babylon." Then it would refer to the Babylonian kings

- Merodach-baladan, reigned 721-710 and again 703-702 B.C.
(He sent messengers to Hezekiah in 712 B.C., cf.
2 Kgs. 20:12-21; Isaiah 39)

- Shamash-shum-ukim, son of Esarhaddon, 681-669 B.C. and
rival brother to Ashurbanipal [669-633 B.C.] who was
made king of Assyria

- a Neo (i.e. "new") Babylon appeared on the scene in 626 B.C.
with the rise of Nabopolassor (626-605 B.C.), the father
of Nebuchadnezzar II (605-562 B.C.). Nabopolassor was
instrumental in the fall of Asshur (one Assyrian capital) in 614 B.C.
and Nineveh (the main Assyrian capital) in 612 B.C..
(see of "Brief Historical Survey of the Powers of Mesopotamia" in Appendix Three).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE DEMONIC IN THE OT

23:15 "for seventy years" The time designation appears here and in Isa. 23:17. It seems to allude to
a complete time (from 7 x 10, see
SPECIAL TOPIC: SEVENTY YEARS).
Notice some of its usages in Scripture.

- revenge, Gen. 4:24

- age of Terah when Abram was born, Gen. 11:26

- seventy in Jacob's family moved to Egypt, Exod. 1:5

- seventy elders during the Wilderness Wandering Period, Exod. 24:1,9; Num. 11:16,24,25
(also Ezek. 8:11)

- number of Abimelech's brothers who were killed, Jdg. 9:56

- expected life span, Ps. 90:10 (double is a special blessing from God, Job 42:16)

- the plague of YHWH killed 70,000, 2 Sam. 24:15; 1 Chr. 21:14

- Ahab's seventy sons, 2 Kgs. 10:1,6,7

- seventy year judgment

- Judah in Babylon, Jer. 25:11; Dan. 9:2; Zech. 7:5

- Tyre, Isa. 23:15

- Jesus sent out seventy, Luke 10:1,17

- forgiveness 70 times 7, Matt. 18:22

▣ "like the days of one king" This phrase designates the expected reign of a monarch. Seventy
years was the time span for a normal life, but here it refers to a very long reign, which probably shows
the symbolic nature of the round number.

23:17-18 The riches of Phoenicia will flow to God's restored people (note also Isa. 18:7 and 45:14,
which denote similar actions). Phoenicia will not respond to the witness of Israel, but will remain pagan
(i.e. Ba'al worship).

The Jewish Study Bible, p. 828, thinks vv. 15-18 are theologically parallel to Isa. 19:18-25, which
describes Egypt and Assyria coming to YHWH. However, the use of "harlot" in vv. 15,17,18 surely points in a different direction.
